analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction employers can claim for spending money to fight union organizing.
analysis.headline: The bill had 108 cosponsors in the House, but it never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers can currently deduct the cost of lawyers, consultants, and captive-audience meetings used to persuade workers against joining a union. This bill would take that tax break away, treating anti-union spending like the already-nondeductible spending that tries to influence the general public about elections. It would also force employers to report that spending to the IRS, with penalties for failing to disclose. The bill never got a hearing or vote and died when the congressional session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to form or join a union. Employers would no longer get a taxpayer subsidy (in the form of a tax deduction) for the lawyers, consultants, and mandatory meetings they use to fight organizing drives, and the public would be able to see how much each employer spends on these campaigns. Unions also benefit indirectly, since raising the cost of anti-union campaigns makes organizing easier.

how_it_helps.text: It denies employers a federal tax deduction for money spent trying to influence their employees' decisions about unions, union elections, labor disputes, and collective bargaining, ending what the bill calls a taxpayer subsidy for those campaigns [S3].

It requires employers to report these expenditures on their tax returns, including dates, amounts, and whether the activity involved an unfair labor practice charge or settlement, with penalties starting at $10,000 or $1,000 per employee for failures to report [S3].

It covers indirect spending too, including wages and administrative costs tied to 'captive audience' meetings where unionization is discussed—though it carves out direct bargaining with a chosen union representative, voluntary recognition, grievance procedures, and legally required postings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers—especially large companies facing union organizing drives—would pay the full cost of their anti-union campaigns rather than deducting it from taxable income, plus new reporting obligations and penalties up to $100,000 for failing to disclose. Some of those costs could in principle be passed to consumers or workers, but the deduction denial is designed to fall on the employer.

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches beyond overt anti-union campaigns: it denies deductions for wages and administrative costs connected to any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed, and for expenses tied to an NLRB complaint or settlement of an unfair labor practice charge, even if the employer disputes the charge (with an exception only if the complaint is later set aside) [S3].

Drawing the line between ordinary management communication about workplace policy and 'attempting to influence employees' about unionization would fall to Treasury regulations, creating compliance uncertainty for employers; the bill directs the Treasury Secretary to issue rules within 240 days of enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real but modest in fiscal terms: it ends a tax subsidy (foregone federal revenue) for employer campaigns against union organizing and shines light on how much employers spend to influence workers, which the bill text itself puts at about $340 million a year on outside consultants [S3]. The cost is a compliance burden on employers and genuine line-drawing problems—deciding which meetings, trainings, and communications count as "attempting to influence" employees—that could create uncertainty for businesses even where no anti-union campaign is underway [S3]. A reasonable objection is that employers have a legitimate interest in communicating with their workforce, and the bill's carve-outs (direct bargaining, voluntary recognition, required postings) only partially resolve how the line would be drawn in practice [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 13, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that spend money to influence their workers' union decisions keep a tax deduction for that spending, with no new reporting requirements. Unions and workers who wanted the subsidy ended gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, citing EPI findings that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in roughly 4 of 10 union elections and spend about $340 million a year on anti-union consultants.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it the only one of 226 House Republicans to support it.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it—no hearing, markup, or vote—before the Congress ended.

against.name: Business and employer-association lobbies
against.role: Business groups opposing restrictions on employer speech in organizing campaigns
against.what_they_did: Would have been the natural opposition, as the bill raises the cost of employer anti-union campaigns; no such activity appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support came almost entirely from Democrats—107 of 216 House Democrats signed on, plus one Republican (Fitzpatrick) out of 226—while no Republican leader advanced the bill in the Ways and Means Committee.

industries.note: Companies would lose the tax deduction for money spent on anti-union campaigns, captive-audience meetings, and consultants, and would have to publicly report that spending with penalties up to $100,000 for failures. The cost of influencing workers' union decisions would fall entirely on the employer.

The bill text cites EPI figures of roughly $340 million a year spent on outside consultants to sway workers' opinions about unions; that spending would become nondeductible and subject to third-party reporting under new section 6039K, making it more expensive and more visible.

Unions themselves are expressly exempted, and by raising the effective cost of employer opposition campaigns, the bill would make union organizing easier—an interest that runs alongside workers seeking representation.
